stem:
A 78-year-old admitted with a chest infection has become quiet and withdrawn. His daughter says he has been a little forgetful for a year but lived independently and was chatty until two days ago. He now answers slowly and says he “can’t be bothered”. Nursing entries record:

| Time | Observation |
| --- | --- |
| 09:00 | Drowsy; drifts off mid-sentence |
| 14:00 | More alert and recognises the ward, but loses track of questions |
| 22:00 | Says there are children at the end of the bed; cannot hold attention |

Which syndrome best accounts for this change?

options.label: A
options.explanation: Withdrawal and ‘can’t be bothered’ suggest depression, but depression does not cause a two-day onset of fluctuating attention and arousal.

options.label: B
options.explanation: A year of mild forgetfulness may be early dementia, which raises the risk of delirium, but dementia progresses over months, not days, and does not fluctuate in arousal like this.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Mild cognitive impairment may describe his baseline, but it cannot account for an abrupt change.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Fluctuating attention and visual hallucinations are core features of dementia with Lewy bodies, which makes it tempting. But that dementia evolves over months; an abrupt change over two days during an infection is delirium, possibly superimposed on an underlying dementia.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Acute onset over two days, fluctuating attention and arousal, drowsiness and perceptual disturbance during an infection are delirium; the quiet presentation is the hypoactive type, often mistaken for depression.

context: An abrupt change with fluctuating attention during an illness is delirium, even when hallucinations or a background of forgetfulness suggest Lewy body or other dementia.
